vignette: At sixty-three, he stands on the sixteenth floor of the Meridian Publishing House when the structural alarms first scream. It is not a quake. The shift supervisor in the loading bay leaves a canister of pressurized industrial solvent improperly sealed, and the spark from a forklift turns it into a fireball. He watches the ceiling tiles rattle like teeth. The smell of burning paper and ozone fills his lungs. He sees three colleagues get pushed backward by the blast wave. He runs down the concrete stairs, throat burning, until he spills out onto the damp pavement with dozens of others, coughing, watching black smoke choke the harbor sky. In the weeks that follow, the trauma does not stay contained. It seeps into his days. He wakes before his wife, Eleanor, does, his chest tight, heart hammering against his ribs as if the blast were still seconds away. The morning news crackling from the kitchen radio sets his teeth on edge. Any mention of industrial safety pulls him under. He checks the gas stove three times before leaving the house, counting the clicks of the pilot light. At the office, he sits near the main exit, his chair angled toward the door. When the building's sprinkler system triggers during a routine test, he drops his pen and curls forward, hands over his ears, breathing in shallow, rapid bursts until the water stops and a junior editor brings him water. He has spent thirty-two years as a publisher, shaping manuscripts, negotiating royalties, and mentoring staff. Now, the work feels like wading through wet paper. The files pile up on his desk, but he cannot bring himself to read the environmental reports he once championed. The cover art for a new coastal development makes his stomach turn; he sees the loading bays, the solvent canisters, the fire. He begins declining meetings in high-rise buildings, suggesting they move to ground-floor cafés or her home study. Eleanor notices how he flinches at the sound of delivery trucks backing up. He tells himself he is merely being cautious, but his hands tremble when he signs contracts. The contracts blur. The deadlines loom. At night, sleep fractures. He dreams of falling paper and screaming alarms, waking at 3 a.m. drenched in sweat, reaching for Eleanor's hand to confirm she is still there. He stops driving past the industrial district, taking long detours through residential streets even when he is late. At a recent literary gala, he stands near the perimeter, eyes fixed on the emergency exits, his jaw clenched. When a waiter drops a tray of glasses, he shoves his chair back, heart racing, until a colleague places a steadying hand on his arm and asks if he is alright. He nods, smiles, says he is fine, and leaves early. Now, he sits across from me in a quiet room that smells of old paper and lavender. He speaks in measured sentences, tracing the line from that morning on the sixteenth floor to the way he now reads his own house like a blueprint for safety. He checks the locks twice. He keeps a flashlight and bottled water in his desk drawer. He has learned to recognize the familiar tightening in his shoulders, the way his breath shallows when the wind shifts, the sudden cold that spreads through his palms when he hears a backfiring engine. He does not call it fear anymore. He calls it vigilance. He sits in the present chair, hands resting on his knees, waiting for the next word to find its place, as he has spent his life arranging words for others.
